html:
The West Baray is a huge rectangular reservoir at Angkor in Cambodia, about 8 km long and 2 km wide, built by the Khmer Empire in the eleventh century. It lies just west of the later walled city of Angkor Thom and is the largest of the Angkor barays.

It was not dug into the ground but made by raising earth banks around a piece of the plain to hold the water. Work probably began in the early 1000s and was finished under Udayadityavarman II, who reigned from 1050 to about 1066. On an island in its centre stands the West Mebon temple, where a great bronze statue of Vishnu was found.

Historians long thought the barays fed irrigation canals and made Angkor's large population possible; the French scholar Bernard Philippe Groslier called Angkor a hydraulic city. Others think they were mainly religious, standing for the oceans around the mythical mountain at the centre of the world. Either way, Angkor's water network was among the largest of the preindustrial world. Unlike the older East Baray, the West Baray still holds water today.
